results.content:
Israeli cybersecurity startup Arrakis Security has raised $8 million in Seed funding to build a platform designed to monitor and govern the behavior of enterprise AI agents, as companies increasingly deploy autonomous systems capable of accessing ...
Israeli cybersecurity startup Arrakis Security has raised $8 million in Seed funding to build a platform designed to monitor and govern the behavior of enterprise AI agents, as companies increasingly deploy autonomous systems capable of accessing sensitive data, executing workflows and making decisions without direct human supervision. Full list of Israeli high-tech funding rounds in 2026
Arrakis Security is betting that enterprises need a new cybersecurity layer focused not just on who has access to systems, but on what autonomous AI systems actually do once they are inside.
The new funding will be used to expand its research, development and product teams in Israel, strengthen its detection and response capabilities, and accelerate deployments among organizations adopting AI agents. The rise of AI agents is creating a new security challenge for enterprises. Unlike traditional software tools, these systems can independently perform tasks, access multiple systems and adapt their behavior based on changing information. Arrakis argues that organizations are facing what it calls a “visibility illusion”: companies may know that an AI agent exists and is connected to a specific system, but often lack a detailed understanding of what the agent is actually doing, which permissions it is using, whether its actions comply with company policies and when normal behavior turns into a security risk.
Rather than focusing only on securing the point where an AI agent enters an organization, such as an endpoint or application, Arrakis is targeting the broader behavior of autonomous systems across SaaS platforms, cloud infrastructure, business applications and internal workflows.

results.name: AI startup Arrakis emerges from stealth with £22.5m round - UKTN
results.content:
London-based industrial AI platform Arrakis has emerged from stealth after securing a $30m (£22.5m) Series A funding round.  
Founded in 2026 by former Accel investor Rafael Quintanilla alongside co-founders Haroun Beltaifa, Romain Fouilland, and Mikhail Galkov, an alumni of Palantir, Delivery Hero, Revolut, Datadog, and ASML, Arrakis develops autonomous AI agents for core workflows across the aerospace, energy, logistics, manufacturing, and telecommunications sectors.  
Arrakis’ model-agnostic platform deploys custom AI agents directly into enterprise systems to automate complex, non-desk operational processes. The company ties a significant proportion of its commercial fees directly to customer performance outcomes.  
Arrakis has already secured enterprise clients, including NYSE-listed industrial and logistics firms, and plans to use the fresh capital to triple its headcount and open new offices in New York and the Middle East.  
“The West is under growing pressure to reindustrialise, but that renaissance won’t be powered by net new companies alone,” said Quintanilla.  
“It requires equipping our industrial champions with the tools to harness their data, navigate the AI transition and compete on a global stage.
“That’s exactly why we founded Arrakis. Most AI investment to date has targeted the 30% of workers behind a desk. The real ROI lies in the 70% running industrial operations. We’re building from Europe for the world, with the ambition to build the Operating System our industrial champions need to win.”  
The Series A round was led by Blossom Capital and saw participation from existing investor Accel, which previously led the startup’s $7.5m (£5.6m) seed round, alongside GFC, MainObject, Rerail, and prominent angel investors.  
“Rafael and the Arrakis team have an exceptional combination of technical depth, operational expertise and commercial ambition,” said Ophelia Brown, managing partner at Blossom Capital.  
“While many companies are focused on AI applications at the edge of the enterprise, Arrakis is tackling some of the most complex operational challenges facing large industrial organisations. Their early traction demonstrates both the scale of the opportunity and the demand for solutions that deliver measurable outcomes.”

results.name: Exclusive: Startup Arrakis emerges from stealth with $38 million in funding to bring AI to industry | Fortune
results.content:
[Arrakis](https://www.arrakis.tech/), a seven-month old London- and Paris-based startup building what it calls an AI “operating system” for industrial companies, is emerging from stealth with $38 million in venture capital funding. It says its goal is to bring agentic AI to sectors such aerospace, energy, logistics, and manufacturing.
The company’s latest funding is a $30 million Series A led by Blossom Capital, with participation from venture capital firms Accel, GFC, MainObject, and Rerail. Accel led an earlier $7.5 million seed round, and individual backers include [Datadog](https://fortune.com/company/datadog/) CEO Olivier Pomel and OpenAI’s head of business products, Olivier Godement.
The latest round values the company at $140 million post-money, cofounder and CEO Rafael Quintanilla told *Fortune.*Quintanilla is a former vice president at Accel. While there, he spent the better part of a year crisscrossing the U.S., Europe, and the Middle East to develop the firm’s thesis on defense and industrial resilience. What he found convinced him to quit and become a founder himself.  
“I realized that there was a huge gap between what I was seeing at Accel and in the Valley, with us investing in companies like Anthropic and Lovable in Europe,” he said, “and what I was seeing in the more industrial parts of the economy.”
He said that most AI has targeted so-called knowledge workers who complete their jobs using software, but that many more jobs in the economy involve the production and movement of physical goods. “Most AI investment to date has targeted the 30% of workers behind a desk. The real ROI lies in the 70% running industrial operations,” he said.  
Sonali de Rycker, the Accel partner who backed Arrakis’s seed round, said she is betting on the founder as much as the market. “Rafa has a rare combination of curiosity, hustle and tireless drive,” she told *Fortune*. “After working closely with Rafa during his time at Accel, it’s an honour to be working with him again as an entrepreneur.”  
But Arrakis is hardly alone in going after manufacturing and industrial firms. Consulting giants such as [Accenture](https://fortune.com/company/accenture/) and Boston Consulting Group are racing into industrial AI, as is [Palantir](https://fortune.com/company/palantir-technologies/), and Jeff Bezos-backed [Prometheus](https://fortune.com/2025/11/17/jeff-bezos-project-prometheus-co-ceo-ai-startup-6-2-billion/)—now valued in the tens of billions of dollars—is pouring capital into automating the engineering of physical products. The frontier labs are circling too.
He said he is skeptical of the sweeping “process transformation” that consultants often sell. “The big project transformation pitch sounds very sexy on paper, and can be great if you want to pump your stock in the short term,” he said, “but what I’m hearing in the boardrooms where I’m sitting is that there is a lot of fatigue from CEOs on having vendors that do not want to commit to short timeline\[s].”  
Instead, Arrakis starts small, he said. For one New York-listed shipping company—which he said he could not name due to non-disclosure agreements—the goal was to improve cash-flow visibility from monthly to daily. Arrakis’s engineers rebuilt the spreadsheet operators already used, having AI populate the data while the system “learns and starts to codify the knowledge of those operators” as they make corrections. The playbook, he said, “always starts with HQ, prove the value, move to field operations as soon as you get the pull to get there.” Arrakis usually charges about half of its fees for hitting a particular performance target, he said.
Landing conservative European industrial firms is its own challenge. Quintanilla offered what he called “an open secret”: his best traction has come from family-controlled businesses. “They think long term, they can push for top-down initiatives to be executed, and I can build non-transactional relationship\[s] with those people.”
